Contentious

/kuhn-TEN-shuhs/ - the stress falls on TEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Contentious means having a tendency to quarrel or dispute.

The historical society schedules the retired colonel last on every program, since the contentious old man will dispute whatever talk precedes his.

Worked Example

Every book club has one. Marguerite arrives with flags in her paperback and challenges ready: the ending was unearned, the hero was not to be trusted, and whatever anyone admires she will gladly contest until the coffee runs out. Nobody escapes: she has disputed the club's snack rotation, its flyer font, and, memorably, the dictionary itself.

Contentious is the exact word because it names a tendency to quarrel or dispute — a standing habit, not a bad night. Marguerite isn't angry and holds no grudges; she simply cannot let a claim go by unquestioned. That itch to contest, wherever it lands, is what contentious describes.

How Contentious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

argumentative

argumentative: loves the back-and-forth of argument; contentious adds a sharper, quarrel-picking edge

disputatious

disputatious: the bookish twin — given to disputing everything

Antonyms

agreeable

agreeable: pleasant and quick to go along

easygoing

easygoing: hard to draw into any dispute at all

How Strong Is It? — opinionated → contentious → belligerent

opinionated vs. contentious

opinionated vs. contentious: An opinionated person is full of firm views but may keep them holstered; a contentious one turns views into disputes.

belligerent vs. contentious

belligerent vs. contentious: Belligerent goes past contentious — from quarreling over points to spoiling for the fight itself.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of contentious.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together, with

Root — tent

Root — tent: to strive, stretch (Latin tendere)

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Con- (together) + tent (to strive, stretch — Latin tendere) + -ious (full of) = full of striving-against. Latin contendere meant to strain with all your force, often against someone straining back. A contentious person keeps that tension handy, stretched and ready for the next dispute.

Use the root in a new word: tension

Use the root in a new word: tension: Tension is the same root at rest — a stretched cord, or a stretched silence before the quarrel starts.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / slightly formal

Contentious is for people (and panels, and families) with a standing tendency to dispute. Its cluster-mates in this unit split the ground: pugnacious wants the fight itself, and fractious is irritable and hard to manage without needing a point to argue. Contentious quarrels have content — a claim to contest. (You'll also meet a contentious issue — one that makes people dispute; the habit is the same, worn by a topic.)
